transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
Iran says that only diplomacy can end the war with the U.S. and Israel.
That's after President Trump rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and
stop the fighting.
NPR's Kat Lonsdorf has more.
In a post on social media, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Iraqchi wrote that Iran was
aware of President Trump's rejection and said that only "negotiated solutions" will end
the conflict now.
He also wrote that Iran is still waiting for an official U.S. response.
Trump told a group of reporters on Saturday that the Iranian plan was not acceptable but
did not give further explanation.
He suggested Iran wanted to make a deal because it's desperate and "losing so badly."
Iran made the proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz at the United Nations General Assembly
in New York last week.
The extended closure of the Strait has caused major disruptions to the world's oil supply.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Five men have been arrested on suspicion of planning to attack a British air base used
by the U.S. military in the Iran war.
NPR's Kristin Wright reports authorities have not named the suspects.
British police arrested the five men after reports of three suspicious vehicles heading
toward the base.
The men are suspected of plotting to carry out a terrorist attack involving explosives
at RAF Fairford in western England, about 100 miles from London.
The U.S. Air Force uses the Royal Air Force base for defensive operations against Iran
and deploys large bombers to launch limited strikes in the war.
President Trump told reporters the suspects were looking to do big damage and had been
watched for a long time.
American troops have used the base for decades under an agreement dating back to the 1950s.
Kristin Wright, NPR News.
A powerful nor'easter remains stalled off New York and New Jersey, pushing water into
coastal communities.
And flood warnings remain in effect today.
NPR's Amy Held reports at least one storm-related death was reported for another reason.
In Brooklyn, a falling tree killed a worker for the New York Housing Authority as wind gusts
topped 60 miles per hour.
More than 100,000 power outages were reported from the Mid-Atlantic to New England.
Some New Yorkers kayaked through flooded city streets.
At the Jersey Shore, some areas saw their highest flooding since Superstorm Sandy 14
years ago.
And Fitzsimmons, owner of Jay's own third restaurant in Stone Harbor, says she and her
team are doing their best to stay afloat.
Everyone is here, all hands on deck.
We're going to get cleaned up.
We've been getting rid of the water.
We have fans running to dry it out.
Forecasters expect repeated rounds of coastal flooding as the system loops offshore before
moving out early in the week.
Amy Held, NPR News.
In Hawaii, a hurricane watch on the Big Island has been lifted.
As NOLO starts to pull away from the islands, forecasters are still urging people to stay
in if possible, as the storm's outer bounds could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
This is NPR News in Washington.
At least a quarter of K through 12 students is missing 10 percent or more of the school
year.
NPR's Janaka Mehta says a new government study says the Education Department needs to do a
better job tracking the problem.
By law, states have to track student absences if they want to receive billions of dollars
in federal funding for schools, because lost days of school equals lost days of learning.
The Government Accountability Office, or GAO, is an independent watchdog.
It found that in 2026, the Education Department stopped doing comprehensive reviews of states
to see if they're following the law in order to get that funding.
It also found problems with the quality of federal data on chronic absenteeism.
The GAO is calling on the Education Department to improve its data and resume its more thorough
monitoring of states.
It says without that kind of oversight, tens of billions of federal dollars could be at
risk of fraud, waste or abuse.
Janaka Mehta, NPR News.
In a visit to France, Pope Leo XIV today drew a crowd of 150,000 to Sunday Mass that he
celebrated at the Shrine in Lourdes, the location known by the faithful for reported episodes
of miraculous healing drew many who were wheelchair bound.
The Pope today spoke out against legislative efforts in France and elsewhere to allow adults
with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medications.
In a visit to a nearby care center, the Pope sought to encourage those who live in an extreme
pain that they have an inherent dignity that no law or algorithm can eliminate.
He also met with French survivors of clergy sexual abuse.
I'm Louise Kievone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Iran says only diplomacy can end war with U.S. and Israel after Trump rejected proposal
Five men arrested in Britain on suspicion of planning attack on RAF Fairford air base
Powerful nor'easter stalls off New York and New Jersey, causing coastal flooding and power outages
Hurricane watch lifted on Hawaii's Big Island as storm NOLO pulls away from islands
At least 25 percent of K-12 students missing 10 percent or more of school year
Pope Francis draws 150,000 to Mass in Lourdes, France, speaks against euthanasia legislation
